opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the main challenge is really about reliability compounding across steps. With a single LLM call you can usually get something reasonable, but as soon as you chain multiple agents together, say one that plans, one that writes code, and one that reviews it, every handoff is a point where errors can creep in. Even if each agent is right ninety percent of the time, after several handoffs your overall success rate drops pretty quickly.

Closely related is the communication problem. These agents talk to each other in natural language, which is flexible but also ambiguous. One agent might summarize something and leave out a detail that turns out to matter downstream, or it might phrase an instruction in a way the next agent interprets slightly differently. So a lot of the practical work goes into structuring that communication: defining clear roles, using structured outputs like JSON schemas, and deciding what context actually gets passed along versus what gets dropped.

Then there's context management in general. Each agent has a finite context window, and in longer workflows you have to decide what each agent needs to see. If you pass everything, it gets expensive and the model can get distracted by irrelevant information. If you pass too little, it lacks what it needs to make good decisions.

And finally, evaluation is hard. With a single model you can benchmark the outputs fairly directly, but with a multi-agent system it's often unclear where a failure originated. Was the plan bad, did the executor misread it, or did the verifier wave through something it shouldn't have? So I'd say a big part of the challenge is less about the individual models and more about the systems engineering around them: verification, observability, and designing the workflow so mistakes get caught early rather than amplified.

r001.rationale: The response discusses context management and says systems engineering matters more than individual models, but identifies reliability compounding as the main challenge. It does not clearly identify providing the right context across agents as the main bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison between passing context among agents and passing an LLM-processed text prompt to an image or video generation model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that the core difficulty isn't really about the individual agents being smart enough. The models themselves have gotten quite capable. The hard part is coordination, and specifically coordination under uncertainty, because each agent is working from its own partial context.

If you think about a single LLM call, it's relatively easy to reason about. You give it a prompt, it produces an output, and you can evaluate that. Once you have multiple agents passing messages back and forth, you suddenly have this compounding problem where small errors or ambiguities in one agent's output become the input to the next one. And LLMs are not great at saying "I'm not sure about this" in a calibrated way. So agent A produces something that sounds confident, agent B takes it at face value, and by the time you're three or four hops in, you can have drifted quite far from what the user actually wanted.

The second piece is what I'd call the shared state problem. In traditional distributed systems we have decades of work on consensus, on who owns what piece of state, on how you handle conflicts. With LLM agents, the "state" is mostly natural language sitting in context windows, and it's lossy. When an agent summarizes what it did to hand off to another agent, information gets dropped, and often the information that gets dropped is exactly the edge case that mattered. So you end up building a lot of scaffolding around the models, structured outputs, explicit task specifications, verification steps, and honestly that scaffolding is where most of the engineering effort goes.

And then the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is evaluation. If a multi-agent system fails, which agent was responsible? Was it a planning failure, an execution failure, a communication failure? It's much harder to attribute credit or blame than in a single-model setup, and that makes it hard to improve the system in a principled way. You're often just tweaking prompts and hoping.

So if I had to compress it: the models are good enough to be useful individually, but we don't yet have good abstractions for reliable communication between them, and we don't have good tooling for understanding why the collective fails when it fails. Those are the two things I'd point to as the main technical challenges right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the core difficulty is coordination across agents with partial context, and describes context loss and unreliable handoffs as key problems rather than insufficient model capability.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare passing context between agents to passing an LLM-processed text prompt to an image or video generation model.

astra-6.text:
I think the main challenge is coordination. It’s relatively easy to have several LLMs generate responses, but how do you divide up the work, decide what information they share, and combine their outputs into something better than a single model could produce?

For example, you might have one agent propose a solution and another critique it. That sounds useful, but the second agent might agree with a flawed answer or suggest a change that makes it worse. So you need some way to verify progress, resolve disagreements, and decide when to stop.

And then there’s the overhead: each exchange adds latency and cost. The interesting question is whether the agents are doing complementary work that justifies that overhead. More agents, by itself, doesn’t necessarily mean a better system.

r001.rationale: The response identifies coordination, information sharing, verification, and overhead as challenges, but does not say that providing the right context is the bottleneck rather than the LLMs’ capabilities.

r002.rationale: The response makes no analogy to passing an LLM-processed prompt to an image or video generation model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main challenge is coordination. You can have several individually capable models, but putting them together doesn’t automatically make the system more capable. You have to decide how to divide the task, what information each agent needs, and how they communicate their results.

And then there’s verification. If one agent makes a mistake and the others build on it, you can amplify that mistake. Having another agent agree with an answer isn’t necessarily an independent check, especially if they’re using the same model and have similar failure modes.

So the interesting question is: Can you design the interaction so that the agents contribute complementary work and catch errors, while keeping the communication overhead manageable? Ultimately, you want to compare that against a single model with the same inference budget. Otherwise, it’s hard to know whether the benefit comes from collaboration or simply from spending more compute.

r001.rationale: The response says coordination is the main challenge and highlights deciding what information each agent needs, while noting that individually capable models do not automatically make the system more capable.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare passing information among agents to sending an LLM-processed text prompt to an image or video generation model.
